title: A Galactic Illusion
caption: The galaxies NGC 4411 and NGC 4410, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
credit: DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys/LBNL/DOE & KPNO/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. Image processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: At the center of this wide view sits NGC 4411, a calm-looking pair of spiral galaxies, with NGC 4411b on the left and NGC 4411a on the right. Above them is NGC 4410, a group of galaxies that are clearly interacting.

NGC 4411 plays a visual trick. The two spirals are thought to be neighbors, both about 50 million light-years from us, but they show no signs of interaction such as distorted arms. NGC 4411a is especially satisfying to look at, with distinct, symmetrical spiral arms that wind more than 360 degrees around its core.

NGC 4410 shows what a real interaction looks like. Its four galaxies are far more tangled and are joined by tidal bridges, streams of material drawn out as the gravity of each galaxy pulls on the others. If the two spirals of NGC 4411 were interacting, they would look similarly intertwined. Their neat, undisturbed shapes show no sign of that, even though the pair are thought to be close neighbors.
scale: Both galaxies of NGC 4411 are thought to lie about 50 million light-years from us, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: DECam on the Blanco telescope observed the galaxies in visible and near-infrared light through g, r, i and z filters. The color mapping isn't published.

explore: The Dark Energy Camera (DECam), built by the Department of Energy, sits at the prime focus of the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at NSF NOIRLab's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory in Chile. It took this image for the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys, which picked targets for the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI).
